_changelog: v1.1.0 (2026-10-14) plain-language pass: every technical word explained where it first appears; options in plain words
title: Letters in a Dead Language

post.author: u/dunholt_lamp_seraphina
post.title: I catalogue manuscripts at night in an abbey's old copying room. Tonight the reading-room screen says our 14th-century psalter was written in the year 212.

blocks.text: I'm the lay archivist at Dunholt Abbey, not a monk. The brothers keep the hours of prayer; I keep the catalogue, the list of every book we hold. Most nights I sit in the old copying room under one lamp and go back over books first catalogued years ago, adding what nobody recorded then. Each entry I save goes out as a message on a Kafka topic, catalogue-entries: a log that keeps every message. Downstairs, the screen in the reading room reads the topic from the start every morning at six and shows visitors what we hold.
The messages are written in Protocol Buffers, a way of turning data into bytes, the small units computers store and send. It's binary: written for machines, not people.

To stay small, a message doesn't carry each value's name, like year. It carries a number instead, the field number. Both sides look that number up in a shared schema, a list saying what each number means. Cuthwin, who has kept the library for forty-one years, calls them letters in a dead language. You can only read them if you know the grammar.

Two developers look after the app from the city. In spring Nkem took the year out of the schema, because a medieval book rarely has one year. He added a text line instead, like c. 1340. Since then the screen has said year unknown for anything I touch, and nobody minded. On Monday Yevgenia added a folio count, the number of leaves.

Their schema registry is a service that checks every new schema before the app may use it. A developer sends it the new schema; it compares it with the last one; if its rules call the change compatible, safe to read, it accepts it. It accepted both.

Tonight, Tuesday, at 01:12 I re-catalogued MS 41, the Dunholt Psalter: Latin, the hand (the handwriting) of about 1340, 212 folios. Then I went down to check the screen, as I always do. It shows a book's shelfmark, its library code, then one line.
READING ROOM   MS 41   Psalter, Latin, written in the year 212
Eleven centuries before anyone wrote it.

I went back up and did two more. MS 7, a Book of Hours of about 1460, 154 folios: written in the year 154. MS 19, an English herbal of about 1420, 96 folios: written in the year 96. Each wrong year is a number I typed tonight, but never into a box marked year.

Cuthwin opened the screen's debug page, a hidden page showing the raw bytes it last read. He copied the psalter's message out by hand, all 35 bytes, as if it were a charter. Each pair of characters is one byte, written in hex, counting 0 to 9 then A to F:

No error anywhere. The screen read every byte and believed it. Yevgenia says the app reads the same bytes back perfectly. Nkem says the screen should have been updated in spring. The brothers open the reading room at nine, and a school party comes at ten.

comments.author: u/grey_pager
comments.text: Before anyone rewrites anything, read Cuthwin's copy the way the screen does. A few words first. A field is one named value in a message, like title or year. On the wire, meaning in the bytes actually sent, each field starts with a tag: one label that packs its field number and a wire type together. The wire type says how to read what comes next. Type 0 is a varint, a whole number written seven bits to a byte (a byte holds eight), so bigger numbers take more bytes. Type 2 is a length, then that many bytes, used for text. A reader works in steps: read the tag, look the field number up in its own schema, read the value the way the type says, then move on to the next tag. Last word: a schema is written in a .proto file, and that file can list reserved numbers, which no field may ever take again. Now the questions. What do the bytes 20 and D4 01 say? What does the screen's copy of the schema call that number, and what does Monday's? Which schema did the registry compare Monday's with, and in which direction? And why did nothing raise an error?

replies.author: u/dunholt_lamp_seraphina
replies.text: Cuthwin worked it out in pencil before I had the laptop open: 20 is field 4, type 0, and D4 01 is 84 plus one 128, which is 212. The screen was built two years ago and still says int32 year = 4 (int32 means a whole number). Monday's schema says optional int32 folio_count = 4. Nkem says the registry's compatibility type, the rule it checks by, is BACKWARD, the default. It checks each new schema against the last one, so that programs on the new schema can read old entries. Nothing else checks. The team that runs the abbey shop's website uses buf, a tool with a breaking-change check. It compares a new schema with the last one released and refuses any change on its list of changes that break programs. Ours never has.

comments.author: u/plain_text_fenwray
comments.text: Binary formats are the problem. JSON, the plain-text format from Season 1, can't do this. In JSON the year travels as "year": 1340 and the folio count as "folio_count": 212. A reader that wants a year looks for the word year and either finds it or doesn't. It can never take a folio count for a date. Sending numbers instead of names is a saving from the days of dial-up, slow internet over a phone line. You catalogue three books a night. Spend the bytes, put the names on the wire, and this whole kind of bug is gone.

comments.author: u/one_night_zuleika
comments.text: The format isn't the bug. The bug is two versions live at once. Nkem changed the writer, the app, in spring, and nobody touched the reader, the screen. Release the app and the screen together, putting both new versions live on one night, from one schema file. Then there's never an old reader to confuse. That's how we do it where I work.

reply.prompt: The brothers want the screen right before the school party, and the developers want to know what to change for good. What do you advise? Part 2 follows your advice.

options.text: Move the topic to JSON, so every entry carries its own field names and no number can be read as the wrong field.
options.verdict: Blanks instead of lies, and no contract
options.part2: Yevgenia moved catalogue-entries to JSON on Wednesday. The screen was rebuilt to read JSON with the schema it had always used, year and all. That night I catalogued the same three books. No impossible years: the screen looked for a field called year, found none, and printed year unknown for the psalter, the Book of Hours and the herbal. The psalter's entry grew from 35 bytes to 94, and the three together from 110 to 287. Nobody noticed the blanks for a fortnight, because a blank looks like a book nobody has dated. And nothing anywhere checked that the app and the screen still agreed on a single field name. Cuthwin says a lie is at least something you can catch.
options.senior: JSON does carry names, so the screen could never read 212 as a year. It showed a blank instead, which is safer but still wrong, and just as silent. The fault was a number reused after a delete, and JSON has the same failure with names. Rename or reuse a name and a reader is misled or left blank. The move costs size, 94 bytes against 35 here. And plain JSON has no schema that anyone enforces. Keep the binary format and fix the contract, the agreement between writer and reader.

options.text: Release the cataloguing app and the reading-room screen together, on one night, so both always run the same schema.
options.part2: The app and the screen were released together on Thursday night, both on Monday's schema. The screen rebuilds its list every morning at six by reading catalogue-entries from the start. And the topic keeps everything, back to entries written before spring with the year in field 4. On Friday morning the new screen read those years as folio counts. The psalter's old entry showed 1,340 folios until the screen reached its new one from Tuesday night. Every book I haven't re-catalogued yet kept a folio count equal to its year. And the nightly copy for the university library, which nobody had remembered, still ran the old schema. It read every new folio count as a year.
options.senior: Releasing together lines up only the programs you remember, at one moment. A topic is a log that keeps old messages. So a new reader still meets data from old writers, and a reader you forgot still meets new data. Schemas have to be readable both ways, old to new and new to old, for as long as old messages and old programs exist. Number 4 meant year in one era and folio count in the next, and no release order fixes that.

options.text: Put new entries on a new topic with the new schema, and move the screen and every other reader across to it.
options.verdict: Right, and a move every time
options.part2: Yevgenia made a new topic, catalogue-entries-2, for Monday's schema, and moved the screen to it on the same schema. That night the psalter read c. 1340, 212 folios, and the Book of Hours and the herbal were right too. The old topic still held two years of entries with the year in field 4. So Nkem wrote a one-off job to copy them across with the year in the dated line, and the university's nightly copy was moved by hand. It took a week. The new schema still listed no reserved numbers. In June Yevgenia asked whether the next deleted field would mean a third topic.
options.senior: A new topic is a clean break. No reader meets a number with two meanings, because the new meaning lives somewhere new. It works, and it is how you handle a change that truly can't be compatible. But it costs a migration, a planned move, every time. Every reader is moved, and old data is copied or read from two places. And nothing stops the new schema freeing a number and reusing it. For one field coming and going, it is a large tool for a small change.

options.text: Reserve number 4, give folios a new number, and add a breaking-change check that refuses unreserved deletes.
options.part2: Yevgenia moved folio_count to 6 and wrote reserved 4 and reserved "year" at the top of the message. When she tried number 4 again in a test, protoc, the tool that turns a schema into program code, refused to build it. Nkem put buf's breaking-change check in the release script, the steps that ship each new version, ahead of the registry. He ran it over spring's change, and it refused it: field 4 deleted without its number reserved. The registry stayed on BACKWARD, as the gate every schema passes through to be used. That night the old screen showed my three books as year unknown: blanks, not lies. The screen moved to the new schema on Friday, and the psalter read c. 1340, 212 folios. Entries from before spring, with the year in field 4, now show folios unknown until I re-catalogue them, never 1,340.
options.senior: In Protocol Buffers the field numbers are the contract, so a number once used means that field forever. Reserving a deleted number makes protoc enforce it. A breaking-change check in the release path stops the next person deleting a field without reserving it. Keep the registry as the gate for publishing schemas. But its BACKWARD check lists removing a field and adding one as compatible, so on its own it was never going to stop this. Old readers still show blanks until a new version of them is put live. And no check sees a change of meaning under the same number.

sim.title: Encode and decode the Dunholt catalogue
sim.lede: You're Yevgenia at a copy of the abbey's setup, with the three books Seraphina catalogued tonight: MS 41 Psalter (about 1340, 212 folios), MS 7 Book of Hours (about 1460, 154 folios) and MS 19 Herbal (about 1420, 96 folios). The cataloguing app encodes each entry with the writer's schema into real Protocol Buffers bytes: for every field a tag (its field number and wire type), then a varint, or a length and the text. The reading-room screen decodes them with its own schema, the reader's schema. A field number it doesn't know is skipped, and a number with no bytes reads as 0, which the screen prints as year unknown or folios unknown. It opens before spring, with both on the old schema. Writer "release 2" means both releases: spring's, which deleted year = 4 without reserving 4, and Monday's, which gave folio_count number 4. Writer "fresh" is the same two releases with 4 reserved and folio_count on 6. You can also send JSON instead, set the registry's compatibility type to BACKWARD (the default) or NONE (checks off), and turn on a breaking-change check that runs before the registry: buf's WIRE rules, which look for changes that break the binary encoding.
sim.tryThis: Try this: set the writer to release 2. The psalter's 35 bytes carry 20 D4 01, field 4, value 212, and the old screen prints written in the year 212; the registry accepted both releases. Switch the format to JSON: no wrong years, three blanks, and 94 bytes instead of 35. Back on Protocol Buffers, set the writer to old and the screen to release 2, as when a new screen replays entries from before spring: 1,340 folios. Set the screen back to old, turn the check on with the writer on release 2, and watch release 1 refused. Then pick the fresh writer, and try the screen on old and on fresh.

explain.oneLine: Nothing aged the books. Number 4 meant year to the screen and folio count to Monday's app. Protocol Buffers sends numbers, not names, so 212 folios arrived as field 4, and the screen read it as the year 212, with no error.

steps.title: Protocol Buffers sends numbers, not names.
steps.text: Turning data into bytes is called serialization, or encoding. The language guide says a field's number "identifies the field in the message wire format" (the bytes actually sent). Encoding one field takes two steps. First the writer writes a tag, which the encoding guide gives as (field_number << 3) | wire_type: the field number shifted up three bits, with the wire type in the three bits left free. Then it writes the value. In the psalter's 35 bytes, 20 is (4 << 3) | 0: field 4, wire type 0, a varint. D4 01 is the varint. The first byte's low seven bits are 84, and its top bit says another byte follows. The second byte is 1, worth 128. 84 + 128 = 212. The words folio_count and year appear nowhere in the message. So if the two sides' schemas disagree about a number, nothing in the bytes can tell them.

steps.title: The screen decoded clean bytes with an old grammar.
steps.text: Decoding, turning bytes back into values, runs the same steps backwards. First the screen reads a tag. Next it looks the field number up in its own schema, which says int32 year = 4. Then it reads the value as the wire type says, and moves on. Monday's schema says optional int32 folio_count = 4. Both are int32, whole numbers sent the same way, so there was nothing for the screen to object to: it put 212 in year. Field 5, the dated line, is a number the screen doesn't know, so it skipped it. Old programs "simply ignore the new field when parsing" (reading), as the guide says. Skipping new fields is what makes adding fields safe. Reusing an old number is what breaks it: the guide says reuse "makes decoding wire-format messages ambiguous".

steps.title: Spring left number 4 free.
steps.text: When you delete a field, the guide says "you must reserve the deleted field number", because "If you do not reserve the field number, it is possible for a developer to reuse that number in the future." A safe delete has two steps. First remove the field from the .proto file. Then add a line like reserved 4; in the same change. After that, protoc, the tool that turns a .proto file into program code, refuses any later field that takes 4. Nkem did the first step and skipped the second. Months later Yevgenia needed a number for folio_count and found 4 free.

steps.title: The registry checked the other direction.
steps.text: Backward compatible means a new reader can read old data. Forward compatible means an old reader can read new data, which is what the screen needed on Monday. Confluent's BACKWARD, the registry's default, checks the first: "consumers using new schema can read data written with old schema (add optional fields, remove fields)". It compares only with the last schema registered. Its check runs in steps. A new schema arrives. The registry compares it with the last one. If every change is on its compatible list, it accepts the schema. Spring removed a field and Monday added one, and both of those are on its list. A breaking-change check asks a different question. buf's rule FIELD_NO_DELETE_UNLESS_NUMBER_RESERVED, in its WIRE category, flags a field deleted without its number reserved. That is exactly spring's change.

steps.title: Three formats, three ways a reader finds a field.
steps.text: JSON is self-describing: the names travel with every value. So the old screen looks for year, finds none, and shows a blank instead of 212, at 94 bytes against 35. Protocol Buffers sends numbers, so it is small, and safe as long as a number never changes meaning. Avro, another binary format, sends neither: its binary data "does not include type information or field names". Its reader works in steps. First it gets the writer's schema, the one the data was written with. Next it matches the writer's fields to its own schema by name. Then it ignores fields it lacks, fills missing ones from its own defaults, or signals an error if a missing field has no default. It needs the writer's schema to read anything, and handing that schema out is a job a schema registry often does.

diagram.aria: The fix. The cataloguing app's schema reserves number 4 and puts folio_count on number 6. Each new schema goes first through a breaking-change check, buf with its WIRE rules, which refuses a field deleted without its number reserved, then through the schema registry on BACKWARD, the gate it publishes through. Entries go to catalogue-entries; the psalter's ends 30 D4 01, field 6. The screen on the old schema skips field 6 and shows year unknown. The screen on the new schema reads folio_count and shows 212 folios.

explain.caption: The fix, drawn for the next release. Number 4 is reserved and folio_count lives on 6. A breaking-change check runs first and refuses any field deleted without its number reserved. The registry stays the gate, on BACKWARD. The old screen skips field 6 and shows a blank, never a wrong year. The new screen reads 212 folios.

fix.title: The fix: reserve what you delete, never reuse a number, and check every schema before it ships
fix.text: Move folio_count to a number that has never been used, 6. Add reserved 4; and reserved "year";, so protoc refuses any field that tries to take them. Put a breaking-change check in the release path, the steps every new version passes through, ahead of the registry. buf's WIRE rules include FIELD_NO_DELETE_UNLESS_NUMBER_RESERVED, which refuses a delete like spring's. If anyone reads the JSON form, the WIRE_JSON rules also refuse a renamed field. Keep the registry as the gate every schema passes through, and know what its compatibility type promises. BACKWARD protects new readers of old data, not old readers of new data. Then move the screen to the new schema.

limits: Old readers still show blanks until a new version of them is put live. With folio_count on 6, the old screen said year unknown for every new entry: no wrong years, but nothing useful either. Reserving a number stops lies, not gaps.

A check sees only what passes through it, and only what its rules describe. A schema copied by hand into another program skips it. And a change of meaning under the same number passes every check, such as counting pages instead of leaves in folio_count.

Registry checks depend on the compatibility type and on what they compare with. BACKWARD compares with the last schema only. Confluent recommends BACKWARD_TRANSITIVE for Protocol Buffers, which compares with every earlier one.

explain.seniorTake: A message format is a contract between programs that are never released at the same moment. And in a log, the old messages outlive the programs that wrote them. So pick a format by what it does when the two sides disagree. JSON fails to a silent blank, Protocol Buffers to whatever the number used to mean, Avro to a default or an error. Then make the contract hard to break by accident. Never reuse a field number, reserve the ones you delete, run a breaking-change check on every change, and let the registry be the gate. Decide which direction you need: new readers of old data, old readers of new data, or both. The compatibility type only promises what its name says.

realWorld.title: Protocol Buffers: the number is the field's identity
realWorld.text: The proto3 language guide (for version 3 of the Protocol Buffers language) says a field's number "cannot be changed once your message type is in use because it identifies the field in the message wire format", and plainly: "Field numbers should never be reused."

realWorld.title: Protocol Buffers: reserve what you delete
realWorld.text: Under Deleting Fields the guide says "you must reserve the deleted field number", because "If you do not reserve the field number, it is possible for a developer to reuse that number in the future." With numbers reserved, "The protoc compiler will generate error messages if any future developers try to use these reserved field numbers." The example reads reserved 2, 15, 9 to 11;.

realWorld.title: Protocol Buffers: compatible types and unknown fields
realWorld.text: The guide lists "int32, uint32, int64, uint64, and bool are all compatible" on the wire, which is why year and folio_count decode into each other without complaint. Adding a field is safe because "old binaries simply ignore the new field when parsing". For a field with no bytes, "For numeric types, the default value is zero."

realWorld.title: The wire format: tags and varints
realWorld.text: The encoding guide says a record's tag is "a varint formed from the field number and the wire type via the formula (field_number << 3) | wire_type". Wire type 0 is VARINT, used for int32 among others, and 2 is LEN, used for strings (text). In a varint "The lower 7 bits are a payload" (the part that carries the number), in little-endian order (lowest part first). Its own example: field 1 set to 150 gives the three bytes 08 96 01.

realWorld.title: Avro: the writer's schema resolved against the reader's
realWorld.text: The Avro specification calls the schema used to write the data the writer's schema and the one the application expects the reader's schema. For records, "fields are matched by name"; a writer's field the reader lacks is ignored; a reader's field the writer lacks takes the reader's default, and "if the reader's record schema has a field with no default value ... an error is signalled."

realWorld.title: Avro: binary with no names at all
realWorld.text: "Binary encoded Avro data does not include type information or field names." The specification says the benefit is small data, but "a schema must always be used in order to read Avro data correctly", and readers "are wholly reliant on the schema used when the data was encoded."

realWorld.title: Confluent Schema Registry: BACKWARD is the default
realWorld.text: Confluent's documentation says "The Confluent Schema Registry default compatibility type is BACKWARD", where BACKWARD means "consumers using new schema can read data written with old schema (add optional fields, remove fields)" and FORWARD means "consumers using old schema can read data written with new schema". NONE means "schema compatibility checks are disabled."

realWorld.title: Confluent: BACKWARD_TRANSITIVE for Protocol Buffers
realWorld.text: The Protobuf page says "In general, it's recommended to use BACKWARD_TRANSITIVE with Protobuf", "as adding new message types is not forward compatible". The transitive types check against all earlier versions, not just the last one.

realWorld.title: buf: breaking-change rules by category
realWorld.text: buf's breaking-change rules come in categories. WIRE "Detects changes that break wire (binary) encoding"; WIRE_JSON "Detects changes that break wire (binary) or JSON encoding"; FILE is the default. FIELD_NO_DELETE_UNLESS_NUMBER_RESERVED, in WIRE and WIRE_JSON, flags a field deleted without its number reserved. FIELD_SAME_NAME, in WIRE_JSON among others, "checks that the field name for a given field number doesn't change", because JSON uses field names.

asked: How do you evolve an event schema without breaking consumers?
interview.answer: Start from who upgrades first. If consumers, the readers, upgrade before producers, the writers, you need backward compatibility: new readers of old data. If producers go first, you need forward compatibility. In a log that keeps messages for a long time, usually both. Then the rules. Only add fields, as optional, with sensible defaults. Never change a field's type or meaning. Never reuse a field number, and reserve the number and name of anything you delete. For formats: JSON is self-describing and easy to look at, but large, and nothing enforces it. Protocol Buffers is compact and identifies fields by number, so numbers are the contract. Avro carries no names or numbers, and matches the writer's schema to the reader's by name, so every reader needs the writer's schema. A schema registry stores every version of a topic's schemas. It checks each new one against a compatibility type before it can be used. Confluent's default is BACKWARD, and it recommends BACKWARD_TRANSITIVE for Protocol Buffers. I'd put a breaking-change check, such as buf, in the release path as well. A registry's compatibility rules and a rule like no unreserved deletes answer different questions.

terms.def: A community of monks or nuns led by an abbot or abbess, and its buildings. Dunholt Abbey keeps a library of old manuscripts.
The monks of Dunholt Abbey.
The fixed times of prayer that a monk keeps through the day and night.
Someone who is not a monk or nun, employed to look after and catalogue an archive. Seraphina is Dunholt's.
The room where monks once copied books by hand, also called a scriptorium. Seraphina catalogues there at night.
A book written by hand. Dunholt's oldest are medieval.
One record describing one book: shelfmark, title, language and when it was made. Each one travels as one message on catalogue-entries.
Catalogue a book again with fuller details. Seraphina is going back over books first entered years ago, adding what nobody recorded then.
A library's code for a book and where it lives, like MS 41.
A book of the Psalms, used for prayer. MS 41, the Dunholt Psalter, is from about 1340.
A prayer book for lay people, arranged by the hours of the day. Dunholt's, MS 7, is from about 1460.
A book describing plants and their uses. Dunholt's, MS 19, is an English one from about 1420.
One leaf of a manuscript, front and back. A folio count says how many leaves a book has: the psalter has 212.
The style of a scribe's handwriting. Experts date manuscripts by it, as in the hand of about 1340.
A formal medieval document, such as a grant of land, written out with great care.
The program Seraphina types entries into. It is the producer: it encodes each entry with its schema and writes it to catalogue-entries.
The Kafka topic the app writes entries to and the screen reads. It keeps every entry, so the screen rebuilds its list each morning by reading from the start.
The display downstairs that shows visitors what the library holds. It is a consumer of catalogue-entries, still built on the old schema.
A hidden page in a program that shows its inner workings, here the raw bytes of the last message it read.
A version of the Protocol Buffers language, declared by syntax = "proto3"; at the top of a .proto file. Dunholt's schemas use it.
A copy of the catalogue the abbey sends a university library each night, made by another program that reads catalogue-entries.
Turning a program's data into bytes to send or store, like packing a parcel, and unpacking it again (deserialization). JSON, Protocol Buffers and Avro are formats for it.
Encode: turn a program's values into bytes, using a schema. Decode: turn bytes back into values, using a schema, which may not be the same one.
What a message looks like as bytes sent over the network or saved on disk, as opposed to inside a program.
The agreed list of a message's fields: their names, their types and, in Protocol Buffers, their numbers. Like a form's layout, both sides need the same one.
A text file in Protocol Buffers' language that lists messages and fields, like int32 year = 4;. Each program's code is made from it.
One value in a message, with a name and a type, like title or year.
The number a schema gives each field, like 4 in int32 year = 4;. Protocol Buffers sends it in the bytes in place of the field's name, like a locker number instead of a name tag.
The label at the start of each field in the bytes: the field number and wire type packed together as (field_number << 3) | wire_type. 20 is field 4, wire type 0.
The part of a tag that says how to read the value after it. 0 is a varint, a whole number; 2 is a length, then that many bytes, used for text.
A whole number written seven bits to a byte, lowest group first. The top bit is set on every byte but the last, meaning more follows. 212 is D4 01.
A whole-number field type in Protocol Buffers, sent as a varint. year and folio_count are both int32, so their bytes look the same.
A text field type in Protocol Buffers, sent as wire type 2: a length, then the letters. Title, language and dated are strings.
A label on a proto3 field so a reader can tell a value never set from a real zero. Spring's dated and Monday's folio_count were added as optional.
Bytes for a field number the reader's schema doesn't have. Protocol Buffers readers skip them, which is why old programs ignore new fields.
What a field holds when its bytes are missing: zero for numbers in proto3. The old screen prints year unknown when year is 0.
A list in a .proto file of numbers and names no field may use again, like reserved 4;. Like retiring a player's shirt number. protoc refuses a field that takes one.
The Protocol Buffers compiler: the tool that turns .proto files into program code. It reports errors, such as a field using a reserved number.
The schema the program that wrote a message used. Here, the cataloguing app's.
The schema the program reading a message expects. Here, the screen's. When it differs from the writer's, something has to settle the difference.
A format whose data carries its own labels, like JSON's field names, so it can be read without a schema.
Apache Avro, a binary format for turning data into bytes. Its data carries no field names or numbers, so a reader needs the writer's schema to read it.
Avro's steps for reading data with a schema other than the writer's: match fields by name, ignore the writer's extras, take defaults for missing ones.
A program on the new schema can read data written with an older one. New readers, old data.
A program on an older schema can read data written with a newer one. Old readers, new data: what the screen needed.
A service that stores every version of a topic's schemas, and checks each new one against a compatibility rule before programs may use it. Like a clerk who checks each new form.
Confluent's schema registry for Kafka. Confluent is a company whose products are built around Kafka.
A registry's rule for accepting a new schema. Confluent's are BACKWARD, FORWARD, FULL, their TRANSITIVE forms, and NONE.
Confluent's default compatibility type: consumers on the new schema can read data written with the old one. It checks against the last schema.
Like BACKWARD, but checked against every earlier schema, not just the last. Confluent recommends it for Protocol Buffers.
The compatibility type that turns the registry's checks off.
A tool that compares a new schema with the last one released and refuses changes on its list of ones that would break readers or writers.
A tool for working with Protocol Buffers. Its breaking-change check sorts its rules into groups: FILE (the default), PACKAGE, WIRE and WIRE_JSON.
Two groups of buf rules. WIRE: changes that break the binary bytes. WIRE_JSON: changes that break the binary bytes or the JSON form, including renames.
A buf breaking-change rule, in WIRE and WIRE_JSON: it flags a field deleted without its number reserved.
A buf breaking-change rule, in WIRE_JSON among others: the name for a field number must not change, because JSON uses field names.
The steps that build, check and ship a new version of a program.
Connecting to the internet over a phone line, slow by today's standards.
A year or folio count the screen shows that is not the book's own, like the year 212 for the psalter.
A year or folio count the screen can't find, shown as year unknown or folios unknown.

atWork: Picture a common incident. A payments team renames a field in an event schema. A consumer still built on the old schema reads the field as missing. It takes the default of zero as the amount, and pays nothing, with no error anywhere. Look for the same in your systems. List every schema your services exchange (.proto files, Avro schemas, JSON contracts) and every reader of each topic. Include exports and analytics jobs, the reports nobody remembers. In each .proto file, check that every deleted field left its number and name reserved. Check your registry's compatibility type for each topic. BACKWARD is Confluent's default, and Confluent recommends BACKWARD_TRANSITIVE for Protocol Buffers. Ask whether your readers upgrade before or after your writers, because BACKWARD only protects new readers of old data. Check whether a breaking-change check runs in your release path before the registry, and with which group of rules. Use WIRE if only binary readers exist, and WIRE_JSON if anyone reads the JSON form. Your company may be working toward ISO/IEC 27001:2022 certification, an outside audit of how it keeps information safe. If so, control A.8.32 (change management) expects changes to information systems to be planned, assessed, tested and documented. A schema check that runs on every change, with a record of what it refused, is the kind of evidence it asks for. So build it into the first schema rather than at audit time.

recall.prompt: Your order service sends OrderPlaced events as Protocol Buffers on a Kafka topic. Six months ago someone deleted the field discount_cents = 7 from the schema. Today a teammate adds gift_wrap_fee_cents, sees that 7 is free, and gives it 7. Three consumers, the programs that read the topic, haven't had a new version put live since before the deletion. What will they do with the new events, and what do you tell the teammate?

keyIdeas.idea: The old consumers decode field 7 as the old discount: a wrong value, silently, with no error, because the bytes look the same
Never reuse a field number: reserve 7 and the old name, and give the new field a number never used
Add a breaking-change check before the registry that refuses deleting a field without reserving its number

recall.model: The three old consumers still have discount_cents = 7 in their schema. A gift-wrap fee is a whole number sent the same way, so they will decode it as the discount: a wrong value, silently, with no error, on every order that has gift wrap. Tell the teammate never to reuse a field number. Give gift_wrap_fee_cents a new number that has never been used. Add reserved 7 and reserved "discount_cents", so protoc refuses the next attempt. Then add a breaking-change check, such as buf's FIELD_NO_DELETE_UNLESS_NUMBER_RESERVED rule, to the release path before the registry. Then a field can't be deleted without its number reserved in the first place.

recall.prompt: A Protocol Buffers message starts with the bytes 08 96 01. What do they say?
options: Field 8, followed by a two-byte value
recall.why: The tag is (field_number << 3) | wire_type, so 08 is field 1, wire type 0, a varint. In 96 01, the first byte's top bit says another byte follows, and its low seven bits are 22. The second byte is 1, worth 128. 22 + 128 = 150. It is the encoding guide's own example. At Dunholt, 20 D4 01 was field 4, value 212.

recall.prompt: A colleague says: "Our schema registry is set to BACKWARD, the default, so any change it accepts is safe for every consumer." On your team, the reading programs usually get their new version weeks after the writing programs. What is wrong with the claim?

keyIdeas.idea: BACKWARD means new readers can read old data; with consumers updated last, old readers meet new data, which needs forward compatibility
It compares only with the last schema version, not every earlier one; transitive types check all
Its list counts removing a field as compatible, so a number deleted without reserving can later be reused; reserve numbers and add a breaking-change check

recall.model: BACKWARD means consumers on the new schema can read data written with the old one: new readers, old data. Your consumers get their new version weeks after producers. So for those weeks old readers meet new data, and that needs forward compatibility, which BACKWARD doesn't promise. It also compares only with the last version, not every earlier one. The transitive types check all of them, and Confluent recommends BACKWARD_TRANSITIVE for Protocol Buffers. And its list counts removing a field as compatible. So a field number deleted without reserving it can be reused later with a new meaning. Reserve deleted numbers and add a breaking-change check in the release path. Compatible to the registry is not the same as safe for every consumer.

recall.prompt: Avro data was written with a writer's schema that has a field year and no field folio_count. The reader's schema has folio_count with default 0, and no year. What does the reader get?
options: folio_count holds the year's value, matched by position
folio_count is 0, and the writer's year is ignored
An error, because the two schemas are different
folio_count is empty, and year is kept as an unknown field
recall.why: Avro matches the writer's schema against the reader's, and for records "fields are matched by name". The writer's year has no match, so it is ignored. The reader's folio_count has no match in the writer's schema, but it has a default, so the reader uses 0. Only a reader's field with no default and no match signals an error. Avro could not have shown Dunholt's year 212.

coldCase.update: UPDATE, 5 months later. Reserved numbers held, and the screen has been right since spring. In March the university library asked for its nightly copy as JSON. So a small program now turns each entry into JSON, using the schema's names. In June Yevgenia changed string language = 3; to string script_language = 3;, renaming the field. The breaking-change check passed it on buf's WIRE rules, the registry accepted it, and the reading-room screen never noticed. Since then every entry in the university's copy says language unknown.
coldCase.prompt: Reply to OP, the original poster. Why did the university's copy lose the language when the screen didn't, and what should the check have been set to?

keyIdeas.idea: The binary wire carries only number 3, which didn't change, but JSON is keyed by name, so the JSON reader looks for language and finds nothing
WIRE rules only protect the binary encoding; with a JSON reader the check should use WIRE_JSON, whose FIELD_SAME_NAME refuses the change
Keep the old name, or add the new field beside it and move the university first before retiring the old one

coldCase.model: In the binary bytes nothing changed: the field still travels as number 3, so the screen decodes it as before. But JSON is keyed by name, and the program that makes the university's copy writes script_language now. The university's reader looks for language, finds nothing and shows a blank. The name changed, and for a JSON reader the name is the contract. WIRE rules only protect the binary encoding, so the check passed it. With anyone reading JSON, run the check on WIRE_JSON, whose FIELD_SAME_NAME rule refuses a field number's name changing. To make the change safely, keep the old name. Or use expand and contract, in steps. First add the new field beside it. Next, move the university to it. Only then retire language and add it to the reserved names.
